title: Can you structure these 9 more growth case questions in two minutes each?
description: 9 more growth case prompts (set 2) to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes, and with this second set the bar rises: each structure should sound as if it could only belong to this client, not to any company that wants to grow. Here are nine more growth prompts, from a football stadium to a payments company. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, say your buckets and where you would start, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
How to use this set

Set a two-minute timer for each prompt. Draw three or four buckets, add two specifics under each, and finish with one sentence on where you would start and why. Then compare with the model, which gives the buckets, the best starting point and the trap.

If you did the first growth set, you will notice the same skeleton underneath: win customers, keep them, earn more from each, or find new sources. This time, push for client-specific language. "Events, tourism, property, community" tells the interviewer you have thought about a stadium; "new revenue streams" tells them nothing.

1. How can a football club make money from its stadium on non-match days?

Show a model structure
  • Events: concerts and other sports; conferences and weddings.
  • Tourism: stadium tours and a museum; the shop and café.
  • Property: a hotel, offices or housing on the site; car parks and retail units.
  • Community: community pitches, gyms and schools; partners and sponsors.

Where to start: events. Concerts bring the largest revenue per day. As a rough hypothesis, ten concert dates at $250k net each would bring $2.5M before event costs and any upgrades.

The trap: ignoring pitch damage, policing and staffing costs, and clashes with the fixture list.

2. How can a department store grow online sales from 15% to 30% of total?

Show a model structure
  • Traffic: search, marketing and the app; existing store customers.
  • Conversion: online range, photos and stock accuracy; checkout and delivery options.
  • Stores as part of online: click-and-collect and returns in store; fulfilling orders from store stock.
  • Repeat: loyalty and personalised offers; delivery subscriptions.

Where to start: stores as part of online. A department store's advantage over pure online rivals is its shops, through click-and-collect and easy returns.

The trap: treating online as a separate business. Also check the maths: if total sales of $1B stay flat, online must double from $150M to $300M.

3. How can a hotel group get more guests to book directly instead of through booking sites?

Show a model structure
  • Price and perks: best rate on our own site and member rates; free breakfast or upgrades.
  • Website and app: ease and speed of booking; search visibility.
  • Loyalty: points and recognition; converting booking-site guests during their stay.
  • Channel terms: commission levels; rate rules agreed with booking sites.

Where to start: converting booking-site guests while they are at the hotel. You already have them; it costs least to persuade them to book direct next time.

The trap: cutting booking sites off before direct bookings can replace the volume.

4. How can a family farm raise its income by 50%?

Show a model structure
  • Yields and costs: output per hectare; fertiliser, fuel and shared machinery.
  • Prices: selling direct and fixed contracts; premiums for organic or local produce.
  • Diversify: a farm shop, tourism and events; renewable energy on the land.
  • Support: grants and environmental payments; co-operatives.

Where to start: diversification. On small farms, side businesses that use the land and buildings often pay better than growing more of the same crop.

The trap: only trying to grow more of the same crop, when prices are set by the market.

5. How can a broadband provider cut customer churn by a third?

Show a model structure
  • Find who will leave: contracts ending and recent price rises; speed problems and complaints.
  • Fix the service: network speed and outages; installation and support.
  • Keep them: retention offers and new contracts; bundles with TV and mobile.
  • Win back: offers to recent leavers; a cancellation process that is clear but caring.

Where to start: predicting who will leave, so offers reach them before the contract ends. To size it: with 2M customers and 18% annual churn, 360,000 leave a year; cutting churn to 12% keeps 120,000 more.

The trap: giving discounts to everyone, including customers who were never going to leave.

6. How can a free personal-finance app start making money?

Show a model structure
  • Charge users: a premium subscription; paid features such as advice or reports.
  • Partners: commission on loans, savings and insurance; switching services.
  • Business customers: selling the tool to employers as a benefit; aggregated insights, with consent.
  • Trust and rules: keeping users' trust; financial regulation.

Where to start: partner commissions. Earning a fee when users take out a financial product is the most common model for free finance apps.

The trap: using customer data in ways that destroy trust, which is the product's real asset.

7. How can a bank grow its lending to small businesses by 25%?

Show a model structure
  • Reach: existing customers who do not borrow; new businesses via partners.
  • Decision speed: time to approve; automated credit checks.
  • Products: overdrafts, loans and invoice finance; pricing against rivals.
  • Risk: expected credit losses; limits by sector.

Where to start: existing customers who do not borrow. The bank already sees their accounts, so it can lend to them safely and cheaply.

The trap: lowering credit standards to hit the target, which shows up as losses a year or two later.

8. How can a software company grow revenue from its existing customers by 20%?

Show a model structure
  • More users: more seats in each account; other teams in the same company.
  • Higher plans: upgrades to premium tiers; add-on modules.
  • Price: annual price rises; pricing linked to value delivered.
  • Keep them: churn and downgrades; customer success teams.

Where to start: more users. Spreading to other teams in accounts you already have is usually the biggest lever. The target is the same as net revenue retention of 120%.

The trap: pushing price rises without adding value.

9. How can a card-payments company win more small shops?

Show a model structure
  • Who we want: types and sizes of shop; those still mainly taking cash.
  • Offer: fees, card readers and payout speed; simple contracts.
  • Channels: online sign-up, partners and banks; regional sales teams.
  • Extra services: lending, booking and stock tools; keeping shops once they sign.

Where to start: the offer. Small shops care most about fees and how quickly they get paid.

The trap: only spending more on advertising.

Make your favourite idea testable

A concert series at the stadium sounds attractive until you add scheduling, policing, staffing, pitch protection and artist fees. The $2.5M estimate is a hypothesis, not a forecast. After sketching any growth structure, pick your most promising idea and say what data would test it: for concerts, available dates, local demand, achievable price, event costs and the effect on the football season.

Then say what would make you drop it. "If we can only free up four dates a year, concerts bring $1M and tours or conferences may beat them" shows the commercial judgement interviewers look for.
